prompt: Which two statements accurately describe RSTP port states? (Choose two.)
options: A designated role proves that a port has already reached forwarding.
A discarding port learns user-frame source MACs but sends no BPDUs.
A discarding port forwards broadcasts while holding unicast frames.
A forwarding port learns source MACs and forwards eligible user frames.
A learning port can learn source MACs without forwarding user frames.
explanation: Learning allows MAC learning but does not yet permit user-frame forwarding. Forwarding supports both; role and state must still be considered separately.

whyWrong.0: A designated port can be discarding while a safe transition is established.
whyWrong.1: Discarding does not learn source MACs from user traffic; it can still process control information.
whyWrong.2: Discarding does not permit ordinary broadcast forwarding.

prompt: Which two statements about designated ports are correct? (Choose two.)
options: A segment selects the port advertising the best spanning-tree information.
On ordinary point-to-point links, the root bridge's active ports are designated.
The designated port is selected by the lowest local interface name on each switch.
Every non-root switch must have exactly one designated port per VLAN.
Two links to the same neighbor always make one local port a backup port.
explanation: A designated port wins the comparison for its segment. On ordinary point-to-point links, the root advertises cost zero and supplies the designated end; shared/self-connected arrangements require the more precise segment rule.

whyWrong.2: Advertised root information, cost, BID, and port ID decide the comparison.
whyWrong.3: A switch can have several designated ports or none; one designated port is selected per segment.
whyWrong.4: Separate parallel links commonly produce root/alternate roles downstream, not a backup role.

prompt: Which command provides a table of root bridge IDs, total root costs, and local root ports across VLANs?
options: show spanning-tree summary
show spanning-tree root
show mac address-table
show interfaces trunk
explanation: `show spanning-tree root` summarizes root information per VLAN. It is useful for comparing instances before inspecting a detailed single-VLAN view.

whyWrong.0: Summary emphasizes mode and defaults rather than the requested root-path table.
whyWrong.2: The MAC table describes learned forwarding entries, not spanning-tree root selection.
whyWrong.3: The trunk display describes VLAN carriage and trunk state, not elected root paths.

prompt: Why can an Ethernet loop keep circulating broadcasts through ordinary Layer 2 switches?
options: An STP root port forwards user traffic independently of its state.
Ethernet frames have no hop limit that ordinary bridging decrements.
Learning a source MAC requires a switch to retransmit every frame.
The enclosed IP TTL is decremented by each switch to limit the frame’s lifetime.
explanation: Ordinary bridging does not decrement the enclosed IP TTL, and Ethernet has no equivalent hop counter. STP removes the loop from the forwarding topology.

whyWrong.0: Both the role and current state matter; a discarding port does not forward ordinary user traffic.
whyWrong.2: Source learning records the ingress location; it does not require universal flooding.
whyWrong.3: Ordinary Layer 2 bridging does not decrement the enclosed IP TTL, so it does not provide that loop limit.

prompt: What does Rapid PVST+ maintain for a network carrying several VLANs?
options: One permanent root elected only when the first switch starts.
A root for each IP subnet, selected from the default gateways.
One root for each physical switch, shared by all its VLANs.
A separate spanning-tree instance and elected root for each VLAN.
explanation: Rapid PVST+ applies rapid spanning-tree behavior per VLAN. Two VLANs can therefore have different roots and forwarding topologies.

whyWrong.0: Election can change when better information or topology changes arrive.
whyWrong.1: Bridge information determines this Layer 2 election; IP gateways do not vote.
whyWrong.2: The instance belongs to a VLAN, not to each switch independently.

prompt: What does this representative VLAN 10 interface excerpt establish about SW3?
options: Gi0/1 is administratively shut, so its cost is ignored by the switch.
Both Gigabit ports forward because both are operational point-to-point links.
Gi0/2 is a backup port because another port uses the alternate role.
Gi0/2 is the current root port, while Gi0/1 is a standby path.
explanation: `Root FWD` identifies the current root port and its forwarding state. `Altn BLK` identifies a healthy alternate that discards user frames for this VLAN.

whyWrong.0: An alternate blocked port participates in STP and is not the same as administrative shutdown.
whyWrong.1: Point-to-point link type does not override the blocked state.
whyWrong.2: Backup and alternate are distinct roles; neither changes the Root label on Gi0/2.

exhibit.title: SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10 — interface excerpt
exhibit.text:
Interface           Role Sts Cost      Prio.Nbr Type
Gi0/1               Altn BLK 4         128.25   P2p
Gi0/2               Root FWD 4         128.26   P2p

prompt: Which conclusion about SW1 is supported by this representative excerpt?
options: SW1 reaches the root through Gi0/1 with total path cost 8.
SW1 is the root because the output identifies protocol rstp.
SW1 reaches the root through Gi0/1 with total path cost 4.
SW1 is the root because its Gi0/1 interface is forwarding.
explanation: The Root ID differs from the local Bridge ID, and the root block identifies cost 8 through Gi0/1. The interface cost 4 is only SW1's contribution to that total.

whyWrong.1: The protocol identifies the STP variant, not which bridge won.
whyWrong.2: The interface row reports the local port cost; the root block reports the total path cost.
whyWrong.3: A forwarding root port belongs to a non-root switch, not the root itself.

Gi0/1               Root FWD 4         128.25   P2p

prompt: For VLAN 20, SW-A has BID 32788.0011.2233.aaaa, SW-B has 28692.0011.2233.ffff, and SW-C has 32788.0011.2233.0001. Which bridge is elected root?
options: SW-B, because its priority field is lower than the others.
SW-A, because its MAC is lower than SW-B's MAC address.
SW-C, because its MAC address is the lowest of the three.
SW-C, because its BID is the last one received by peers.
explanation: SW-B wins because 28692 is lower than 32788. The MAC portion is compared only after the priority/system-ID field ties.

whyWrong.1: SW-A has a higher priority field, so its MAC is not the deciding comparison.
whyWrong.2: The lower MAC cannot override a worse priority field.
whyWrong.3: BPDU arrival order does not replace the best-BID comparison.

prompt: All VLAN 10 switches use default configurable priority 32768. After `spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary` is entered on SW2, which displayed priority should be expected?
options: 32778, because the macro changes only a role label.
24576, because the VLAN ID is omitted from Root ID.
28682, from configurable priority 28672 plus VLAN 10.
24586, from configurable priority 24576 plus VLAN 10.
explanation: With the stated default-priority peers, the macro sets 24576. The per-VLAN displayed field includes the extended system ID, producing 24586 for VLAN 10.

whyWrong.0: The macro changes a numeric priority setting rather than granting a special role.
whyWrong.1: 24576 is the configurable component; the displayed field includes VLAN 10.
whyWrong.2: 28672 is the secondary macro value, not the primary value in this scenario.

prompt: Both candidates advertise the same root. Using the given costs, which interface should SW4 select as its root port?
options: Fa0/24, because the route uses fewer switch links.
Gi0/1, because received cost 4 plus local cost 4 is 8.
Gi0/1, because its local interface number is lower.
Fa0/24, because its neighbor is the root itself.
explanation: The candidate via Gi0/1 costs 4 + 4 = 8; the direct Fa0/24 candidate costs 0 + 19 = 19. Root-port selection prefers the lower total cost, before any port-ID tie-breaker.

whyWrong.0: STP uses path cost rather than a simple hop count.
whyWrong.2: The choice is established by cost before interface IDs are compared.
whyWrong.3: Direct attachment does not beat a lower-cost indirect path.

exhibit.title: SW4 worksheet — VLAN 10
exhibit.text:
Candidate   Received root cost   Local port cost
Fa0/24      0                    19
Gi0/1       4                    4

prompt: SW1 has equal-cost direct links to the same root bridge. Gi0/1 receives sender port ID 128.26; Gi0/2 receives 128.25. Which interface wins?
options: Gi0/2, because its received sending-port identifier is lower.
Neither port, because parallel links require an EtherChannel.
Gi0/1, because SW1's lower local interface number decides first.
Both ports, because equal-cost links share the root-port role.
explanation: Root ID, total cost, and sender BID tie, so the sending port ID decides. Gi0/2 hears 128.25, which is better than 128.26 even though its local interface name is higher.

whyWrong.1: Parallel links can operate under STP without an EtherChannel; one can be alternate.
whyWrong.2: The sender port ID is compared before the local receiving port ID.
whyWrong.3: A non-root bridge selects one root port per instance.

prompt: An interswitch link is using classic interoperability behavior after a replacement switch was installed. Which change aligns the replacement with the intended rapid design?
options: Lower the replacement's VLAN priority to reserve the root role.
Force the replacement's uplink to shared link type for safety.
Configure `spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst` on the replacement.
Enable PortFast on both ends of the interswitch transit link.
explanation: The replacement reports PVST mode, which uses classic behavior. Configuring the intended rapid mode addresses that mismatch; verify the operational peer behavior after protocol negotiation rather than assuming a fixed recovery time.

whyWrong.0: Priority controls root election, not rapid versus classic protocol operation.
whyWrong.1: Shared link type prevents the point-to-point rapid handshake rather than enabling it.
whyWrong.3: PortFast is not the remedy for a transit-link protocol mismatch.

exhibit.title: Replacement SW2# show spanning-tree summary — excerpt

prompt: An engineer changes SW1 Fa0/24 to `spanning-tree vlan 30 cost 2`. What is the direct effect, and how can it affect other switches?
options: The root bridge changes its BID to include 2; every switch repeats that new BID.
The peer changes its receiving port cost to 2; SW1 keeps its own automatic cost.
SW1 raises the physical link speed; neighboring switches learn the new bandwidth.
SW1 uses cost 2 for that candidate; a changed advertised root cost can affect neighbors.
explanation: The interface command changes SW1's VLAN 30 path-cost contribution on that port. If this changes its selected root cost, updated advertisements can influence downstream root or designated-port decisions.

whyWrong.0: Cost and BID are different fields; this command does not change bridge priority or MAC.
whyWrong.1: The command is local to SW1; it does not configure the peer's interface cost.
whyWrong.2: STP cost is a selection parameter and does not change physical bandwidth.

prompt: The physical link stays up, but an RSTP port misses three consecutive BPDUs with a two-second hello interval. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The bridge must wait exactly 50 seconds before detecting the missing neighbor.
The bridge has proved the fiber transmit strand is physically broken.
The bridge can age the neighbor information after about six seconds.
The bridge guarantees that all application traffic recovers in six seconds.
explanation: Three missed two-second hellos correspond to about six seconds and allow rapid aging of neighbor information. Detection does not identify the physical cause or guarantee a specific end-to-end recovery duration.

whyWrong.0: Classic worst-case timer examples are not the required rapid neighbor-detection behavior.
whyWrong.1: Several faults can stop BPDUs while link status remains up.
whyWrong.3: Neighbor detection and complete traffic recovery are separate events.

prompt: A new switch has VLAN 10 priority 4096. Existing root SW1 was selected using the primary macro and has the shown configured setting. With no guards, what happens?
options: The new switch wins because its configured priority is lower than 24576.
SW1 retains the role because the macro permanently marks it as primary.
SW1 automatically subtracts 4096 from the newcomer's advertised priority.
The new switch waits for SW1 to fail before it may participate in elections.
explanation: The macro left an ordinary priority setting of 24576. The new switch's lower priority gives it the better BID for the same VLAN; the macro does not keep monitoring and reducing SW1's priority.

whyWrong.1: Primary is a configuration convenience, not a permanent protocol privilege.
whyWrong.2: There is no ongoing adjustment process attached to the earlier macro invocation.
whyWrong.3: All participating bridges compare BIDs; no reservation forces the newcomer to wait.

exhibit.title: SW1 running-config excerpt
exhibit.text:
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 24576

prompt: Two ports of the same switch attach to one shared hub segment. One receives the switch's own superior BPDU and provides a redundant attachment to its designated port. Which role describes that port?
options: Backup, because it backs up this bridge's attachment to the same segment.
Designated, because each local interface must advertise onto the hub.
Alternate, because every redundant cable provides a path through another bridge.
Root, because a received BPDU always selects the path toward the root.
explanation: A backup port is associated with a redundant connection to the same segment served by the bridge's own designated port. An alternate instead provides another path toward the root through a different bridge.

whyWrong.1: The segment selects one designated port; redundant local attachments need not both be designated.
whyWrong.2: The stated BPDU comes from the same bridge, not a different bridge on another path.
whyWrong.3: Receiving a BPDU alone does not establish the root-port role.

prompt: SW-A and SW-B advertise the same root with root path cost 8 on their connecting segment. Which end becomes designated based on the worksheet?
options: SW-B, because its sending bridge ID is lower at the tied advertised cost.
SW-A, because its port number is lower than SW-B's port number.
SW-A, because its local interface cost of 4 is lower.
SW-B, because designated-port selection prefers the higher link cost.
explanation: For the designated-port comparison, both advertise cost 8, so the sending BID decides. SW-B has the lower BID; the segment's local receiving cost is not added to the already advertised cost for this comparison.

whyWrong.1: Sender BID is compared before sender port ID.
whyWrong.2: The local cost would matter when evaluating a received root-port candidate, not as a new designated-port tie-breaker here.
whyWrong.3: There is no rule preferring a higher port cost; SW-B wins on BID.

Advertised cost  8                     8

SW-A BID: 30.00aa.0000.0001

Both belong to the same connected VLAN 30 instance.

prompt: Both VLAN 30 candidates use configurable priority zero. Which result follows from the complete BIDs?
options: SW-A wins because priority zero prevents any other root claim.
They retain separate roots because both configurable priorities are zero.
SW-A wins because the MAC comparison prefers the higher value.
SW-B wins because its MAC is lower after the priority fields tie.
explanation: Both displayed priority fields are 30. SW-B has the lower MAC, so it has the lower complete BID. Zero does not guarantee permanent root status.

whyWrong.0: The MAC still breaks a priority tie.
whyWrong.1: Connected participants compare complete BIDs and converge on one root for the instance.
whyWrong.2: The lower MAC wins the tied-priority comparison.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
Same root ID received on both ports.
Gi0/1: advertised cost 4; local cost 4; sender BID 32778.0001.0000.0001; sender port 128.1
Gi0/2: advertised cost 4; local cost 4; sender BID 28682.00ff.0000.0001; sender port 128.48

prompt: The candidates advertise the same root and produce equal total cost. Which SW-C port becomes the root port?
options: Gi0/1, because the sender port number is lower.
Gi0/2, because the sending bridge ID is lower.
Both, because equal-cost spanning-tree paths are load shared.
Gi0/1, because the local receiving port number is lower.
explanation: Both totals are 8. Sender BID is compared before either sender port ID or local receiving port ID, so the lower-priority sender on Gi0/2 wins.

whyWrong.0: Sender BID already resolves the tie before sender port ID.
whyWrong.2: A non-root switch chooses one root port per instance; these are not an EtherChannel.
whyWrong.3: The local port is a later tie-breaker and is not reached.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
Rapid PVST+; VLANs 10 and 20 present and allowed on all triangle links A-B, A-C, B-C.
All receiving costs are 4 for both VLANs.
VLAN 10 priorities: A 24576, B 28672, C 32768.
VLAN 20 priorities: A 28672, B 24576, C 32768.

prompt: C has direct links to A and B and no other links. What should C use as its root port in each VLAN?
options: C-A for both VLANs because the lower VLAN number wins the election.
C-B for both VLANs because B is a root in one instance.
Both physical links in both VLANs because each VLAN needs two root ports.
C-A in VLAN 10 and C-B in VLAN 20, based on the separate instances.
explanation: Each VLAN compares its own root information. The direct path to its intended root costs 4; crossing the other switch would cost 8. One physical interface can have different roles in different VLANs.

whyWrong.0: VLAN numbers do not compete against each other in a single election.
whyWrong.1: B’s VLAN 20 root role does not make it the VLAN 10 root.
whyWrong.2: C selects one root port in each instance, not both.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
Same VLAN 10; both local port costs 4; no guards.
Gi0/1 advertises root BID 32778.0001.0000.0001, advertised cost 0.
Gi0/2 advertises root BID 24586.00ff.0000.0001, advertised cost 100.

prompt: A switch receives these two advertisements. Which root identity is preferred before comparing paths to the same root?
options: Both identities remain roots because their advertised costs differ.
The advertisement on Gi0/1, because advertised cost zero beats cost 100.
The advertisement on Gi0/1, because the receiving port number is lower.
The advertisement on Gi0/2, because it identifies the lower root BID.
explanation: Root identity is compared before cost. A high-cost path to the better root is preferred to information naming a worse root; later comparisons choose the best path to that selected root.

whyWrong.0: Different costs do not authorize two roots in the same connected instance.
whyWrong.1: Cost does not override a better root identity.
whyWrong.2: Port-number comparison is much later in the decision.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
One VLAN 10; all links bidirectional point-to-point.
Configurable priorities: A 24576; B 28672; C 32768.
A-B cost: 4 at each end.
B-C cost: 4 at each end.
A-C cost: 19 at each end.
No guards, bundles, manual overrides beyond these costs, or other links.

prompt: After this complete triangle converges, which combined description is correct?
options: B uses B-C at cost 23; C uses C-A at cost 19; B-A is alternate at B.
B and C both use direct root links; A blocks its higher-cost A-C port.
B uses B-A at cost 4; C uses C-B at cost 8; C-A is alternate at C.
B uses B-A at cost 4; C uses C-A at cost 19; C-B is alternate at C.
explanation: A has the lowest BID. B reaches A at cost 4. C compares 19 directly with 4 + 4 through B and chooses 8. A advertises zero on A-C, so A remains designated there and C discards on its alternate.

whyWrong.0: B has a direct cost-4 path and does not select cost 23.
whyWrong.1: The root advertises cost zero and is designated on both ordinary point-to-point links; the non-root end supplies the alternate.
whyWrong.3: C chooses the cheaper 8 path, not the fewer-hop path costing 19.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
One VLAN 10 triangle; no guards or other links.
Original priorities: A 24576; B 28672; C 32768.
A-B: cost 4 at each end; B-C: cost 4 at each end; A-C: cost 19 at each end.
Change: B priority becomes 4096. A and C priorities remain unchanged.

prompt: B changes only its VLAN 10 priority to 4096. Which new stable result follows?
options: A and C each reach B at cost 4; A is designated on the A-C segment.
A reaches B through C at cost 23; C becomes designated on A-C.
A stays root because its previous configured priority was lower than C.
C reaches B through A at cost 23, and A-C is forwarding at both ends.
explanation: B now has the lowest BID. A and C each have a direct cost-4 root path. Their advertised costs tie on A-C, so A’s lower BID wins designated and C’s end becomes alternate.

whyWrong.1: A also has a direct cost-4 link; A’s lower BID wins the separate designated comparison.
whyWrong.2: B’s new configurable 4096 is lower than A’s 24576.
whyWrong.3: C has a direct cost-4 link to the new root and does not choose 23.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
One VLAN 10, no guards or other links.
Priorities: A 24576; B 28672; C 32768.
Initial symmetric costs: A-B 4; B-C 4; A-C 19.
Only C’s receiving cost on C-A changes to 2; A’s cost on A-C stays 19.

prompt: A remains the root. C changes only its receiving cost on C-A from 19 to 2. Which pair of changes is expected after convergence? Choose two.
options: A loses the root role because C now advertises a smaller cost.
C selects C-A as its root port with total cost 2.
The physical C-A bandwidth increases to match the lower cost.
B becomes alternate on B-C, while C is designated there.
B changes its root path to B-C-A with total cost 6.
explanation: C’s direct cost 2 beats its previous 8 path. B retains direct cost 4 because its route through C costs 4 + 2 = 6. On B-C, C advertises 2 against B’s 4, so the designated end changes to C.

whyWrong.0: A remains the best BID and advertises root cost zero.
whyWrong.2: An STP cost override changes preference, not link bandwidth.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
Plan: PC-A and PC-B in VLAN 10, 10.0.10.11/24 and 10.0.10.12/24.
Actual PC addresses/masks match. PC-A connects to SW1 Fa0/5.
SW1 VLAN 10: Gi0/1 Root FWD; Fa0/24 Altn BLK.
All links on the Gi0/1 forwarding path carry VLAN 10 to PC-B.
SW1 show vlan brief: VLAN 20 includes Fa0/5; PC-B port is in VLAN 10.

prompt: PC-A cannot reach PC-B. Which correction is supported while preserving the intended spanning tree?
options: Lower SW1’s priority until both interswitch ports have a designated role.
Change PC-B’s mask so frames avoid the blocked SW1 interface.
Reassign PC-A’s port to VLAN 10, then retest through the existing forwarding path.
Disable spanning tree on Fa0/24 so both interswitch paths forward VLAN 10.
explanation: The tree provides an active VLAN 10 path, but PC-A’s actual access membership is VLAN 20 despite the plan. Correct that specific mismatch and retest. A normal alternate is not evidence that STP caused the outage.

whyWrong.0: Changing the root cannot put PC-A into the intended VLAN.
whyWrong.1: The host masks already match the addressing plan; the demonstrated error is access membership.
whyWrong.3: Forcing redundant paths to forward can reintroduce a loop and does not correct host membership.

exhibit.title: Supplied spanning-tree worksheet
exhibit.text:
One VLAN 10 triangle before failure: A 24576, B 28672, C 32768.
PC-A is attached only to A; PC-C only to C.
Both PCs are in the same VLAN and subnet. No other devices or links exist.
Failed links: A-B and A-C. Healthy link: B-C.

prompt: Root A loses both of its interswitch links, but remains powered with PC-A attached. B-C stays up. Which outcome follows for VLAN 10?
options: C becomes root of B-C because its priority is numerically greater.
B becomes root of the B-C component, but PC-A is isolated from PC-C.
B becomes root of all three switches, and PC-A uses its default gateway.
A remains the common root and PC-A reaches PC-C through B-C.
explanation: The disconnected network now has separate components. B has the better BID among B and C, so C reaches B. No remaining cable joins PC-A’s component to PC-C’s, regardless of the successful B-C election.

whyWrong.0: The lower priority wins: B 28672 beats C 32768.
whyWrong.2: B cannot provide a common tree across disconnected components, and a gateway does not create a missing physical path.
whyWrong.3: No control or data path remains between A and the other switches.
